_readme: Copy this file to browser-targets.local.json and fill it in. That name is
gitignored, which is the point: the hostnames of your employer's or your
client's environments must not enter a public repo. Same pattern as
.env.example beside a gitignored .env.
scripts/bash-guard.py reads it to decide which hosts curl and browser
automation may reach. localhost, *.local and *.test are always allowed and
do not belong here. With no file present the guard allows only those, so a
fresh clone on someone else's machine reaches nothing of yours.
allowed_suffixes: whole zones. Every entry MUST start with a dot, because
the match is endswith() and the leading dot is the only thing making it a
label boundary: 'evil-env-dev.contoso.com' does not end with
'.env-dev.contoso.com'.
Two labels minimum, so '.com' cannot be entered. Use this only for a zone
that holds nothing but lower environments.
allowed_hosts: exact hostnames, compared with ==. Use this, never a suffix,
for any zone that holds production and lower environments together. If
api.contoso.com is production and api-test.contoso.com is not, then
'.contoso.com'
in allowed_suffixes would allow production, and that is the one thing that
must never happen. Listing exact hosts means a new subdomain stays denied
until someone adds it deliberately.
Leave out anything holding production-like data. A staging environment
restored from a production snapshot is production data with a friendlier
name. Do not put an IP range or an IPv6 literal in either list; suffix
matching cannot express either one correctly.
Entries must be lowercase ASCII. Anything malformed is dropped silently
rather than widening the allowlist.
